noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to use experimental data to calculate empirical and molecular formulae

primer.text: Experimental data knows percentages and masses, not formulae. This note converts composition into empirical formulae by divide-by-smallest arithmetic, upgrades them to molecular formulae through the relative mass ratio, weighs elements inside compounds as percentages, and computes water of crystallisation from the mass a hydrate loses on heating.

lessons.title: Empirical to molecular
lessons.opening: Experimental masses or percentages are the raw material of formula work. This lesson builds the two-step routine - divide by atomic masses, then scale by the smallest ratio - and then upgrades the empirical formula to the molecular one using the relative formula mass.
keyPoints: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of each element.
Divide each element's mass (or % mass) by its relative atomic mass, then divide every answer by the smallest to force whole numbers.
The molecular formula is the empirical formula multiplied by an integer n.
n = Mr(molecular) / Mr(empirical); for C4H10S with Mr 180.2, n = 180.2 / 90.1 = 2.

low.restatement: Turn masses into moles, divide by the smallest, and the whole numbers that fall out are the subscripts.
low.analogy: It is like simplifying 6:9 to 2:3 - the recipe stays recognisable but the counts shrink to the simplest form.
low.examPointer: Table your working in columns: mass, Ar, moles, ratio. Method marks live in that table.

medium.restatement: Mass-to-moles division measures each element in the same unit (moles), so their quotient is the atom ratio; multiplying the empirical unit by n inflates it to the real molecule whose relative mass matches experiment.
medium.analogy: The empirical formula is the scale drawing; the molecular formula is the full-size build, n times larger in every dimension.
medium.examPointer: If the ratio lands near 1.5, double it to 3 - experimental rounding, not a new element, explains the fraction.

check.stem: What does an empirical formula state?

options.text: The simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element
options.explanation: Ratios are reduced to the smallest whole numbers.

options.text: The exact atom count in one molecule
options.explanation: That is the molecular formula.

options.text: The charge balance inside the compound
options.explanation: Formulae record atom ratios, not charges here.

options.text: The mass fraction of each element
options.explanation: Mass fractions are the input data, not the formula output.

check.stem: A sample is made of 10 g hydrogen mixed with 80 g oxygen. After dividing by Ar values (H = 1.0, O = 16.0), the mole counts are 10 and 5. What is the empirical formula?

options.explanation: Dividing by the smallest (5) leaves H:2 and O:1.
The ratio 10:5 reduces to 2:1, not 1:1.
That would need equal mole counts.
Empirical formulae are reduced, not carried forward.

check.stem: The empirical formula of X is C4H10S and its relative molecular mass is 180.2. What is n, given the empirical mass works out at 90.1 from carbon 12.0, hydrogen 1.0 and sulfur 32.1?

options.explanation: 180.2 / 90.1 = 2, so the molecule is two empirical units.
A factor of 1 would make Mr equal 90.1.
That would need Mr near 360.
n must be a whole number of units.

check.stem: Why can the empirical formula and the molecular formula coincide?

options.text: When the molecular formula is already in its simplest whole-number ratio
options.explanation: If n = 1, the two formulae are identical, as for water.
Ionic formula units are ratios anyway, but coincidence is about n, not bonding type.

options.text: When percentages are used instead of masses
options.explanation: The data source does not decide the outcome.
Water, ammonia and methane all have identical empirical and molecular formulae.

check.stem: A ratio calculation gives C:1.5, H:3, O:1. What should you do?

options.text: Double all values to reach whole numbers: C2H6O
options.explanation: Half-values signal a doubling step, not a fractional atom.
Rounding distorts the ratio; scale instead.

options.text: Report the empirical formula with decimals
options.explanation: Empirical formulae are whole-number ratios by definition.
The data may be fine; the ratio needs scaling.

check.stem: State the two-step routine that turns percentage composition into an empirical formula.
check.modelAnswer: Divide each percentage by the element's relative atomic mass to get mole proportions, then divide every proportion by the smallest to obtain the whole-number ratio.

check.stem: State how a molecular formula follows from an empirical formula.
check.modelAnswer: Compute n = Mr(molecular) / Mr(empirical) and multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by n.

check.stem: Explain why dividing every mole count by the smallest count is the step that produces the empirical formula.
check.modelAnswer: Dividing by the smallest mole count forces the least abundant element to 1, and since all counts are divided by the same number, the ratio is unchanged but expressed in the smallest whole-number terms - the definition of the empirical formula.

check.stem: Determine the molecular formula of X whose empirical formula is C4H10S and whose relative molecular mass is 180.2, using Ar values: carbon 12.0, hydrogen 1.0 and sulfur 32.1.
check.modelAnswer: Empirical mass = (4 x 12.0) + (10 x 1.0) + 32.1, giving 90.1; n = 180.2 / 90.1 = 2; molecular formula = C8H20S2.

lessons.title: Weighing an element inside a compound
lessons.opening: Percentage composition runs the formula routine backwards: given the formula, what fraction of the mass belongs to each element? This lesson installs the % mass equation and works calcium carbonate end to end.
keyPoints: % mass of an element = (Ar x atom count) / Mr(compound) x 100.
The numerator counts every atom of that element in the formula unit.
For CaCO3, calcium's share is 40.1 / 100.1 x 100, about 40.1%.
Percentage composition data can also be read in reverse to feed empirical formula work.

low.restatement: Take the element's total mass in one formula unit, divide by the formula's total mass, and multiply by 100.
low.analogy: Like working out what fraction of a cake's cost is the butter: one ingredient's bill over the whole shopping list.
low.examPointer: Multiply by the atom count BEFORE dividing - forgetting the count is the common mark-loss.

medium.restatement: The ratio (Ar x n)/Mr is dimensionless because both numerator and denominator carry the same relative-mass units, so multiplying by 100 gives a clean percentage.
medium.analogy: It is a pie chart in equation form: each element's slice of the formula's total mass.
medium.examPointer: All percentages in one compound must sum to 100 (within rounding) - a quick self-check.

check.stem: Which expression gives the percentage by mass of element E in a compound?

options.text: (Ar(E) x atoms of E) / Mr x 100
options.explanation: The element's total relative mass over the formula mass, scaled to 100.
Omitting the atom count undercounts elements appearing multiply.
That inverts the fraction and exceeds 100 for most elements.

options.text: atoms of E / total atoms x 100
options.explanation: Atom counts are not mass fractions.

check.stem: What share of calcium carbonate's mass belongs to calcium? (Ar: Ca 40.1, C 12.0, O 16.0; Mr = 100.1)

options.explanation: That is oxygen's share (3 x 16.0 = 48.0).
That is carbon's share.
Half the true value; the numerator was halved.

check.stem: Why must the atom count of the element appear in the % mass numerator?

options.text: Each atom of the element contributes its Ar to the compound's total mass
options.explanation: Two oxygens contribute 2 x 16.0, so the count multiplies the Ar.

options.text: Because Ar values are percentages already
options.explanation: Ar values are relative masses, not percentages.
The equation stays in mass terms throughout.
Ar already averages isotopes; the count is a separate factor.

check.stem: A compound's percentages sum to 99.7% after rounding. What does that tell you?

options.text: The data are consistent within rounding; the sum should approach 100%
options.explanation: Rounding at 3 s.f. can leave a small residue below 100.

options.text: An element is definitely missing from the analysis
options.explanation: A 0.3% residue is normal rounding, not a missing element.
Percentage sums do not validate formulae by themselves.
Nothing about the sum implies a scaling error.

check.stem: Which compound has the HIGHER percentage by mass of oxygen: H2O (Mr 18.0) or CO2 (Mr 44.0)? (Ar of O = 16.0)

options.explanation: CO2 carries 32.0/44.0; water carries 16.0/18.0 = 88.9%... careful - water's share is higher, so check: 16/18 = 88.9% beats 32/44 = 72.7%, so the correct answer is H2O.
The shares differ by 16 percentage points.

options.text: CO2, because it holds two oxygens
options.explanation: The extra oxygen still divides by a bigger total mass.

check.stem: State the equation used to compute an element's percentage share of a compound's mass.
check.modelAnswer: % mass = (relative atomic mass of the element x number of its atoms) / relative formula mass of the compound x 100.

check.stem: State the percentage by mass of oxygen in water (Ar of O = 16.0, Mr = 18.0).
check.modelAnswer: 16.0 / 18.0 x 100 = 88.9% (3 s.f.), the largest share of the molecule's mass.

check.stem: Explain why percentage by mass and percentage by atom count give different rankings for the same compound.
check.modelAnswer: Mass percentages weight each element by its relative atomic mass, so a heavy atom counts more than its population suggests, while atom-count percentages treat every atom equally; hydrogen in water is 2 of 3 atoms but only 11% of the mass because each hydrogen atom is so light.

check.stem: Calculate the percentage by mass of sulfur in sulfuric acid, H2SO4 (Ar: H 1.0, S 32.1, O 16.0; Mr = 98.1).
check.modelAnswer: Sulfur contributes 32.1 of the 98.1 total: % = 32.1 / 98.1 x 100 = 32.7% (3 s.f.).

lessons.title: Water of crystallisation
lessons.opening: Some crystals smuggle water into their structure as part of the formula. This lesson reads dot formulae like CuSO4.5H2O, contrasts hydrated with anhydrous salts, and computes the degree of hydration from a heating experiment.
keyPoints: Water of crystallisation is water built into a crystal's structure as part of the formula, written after a dot.
A hydrated compound carries that water; an anhydrous one does not.
Heating drives the water off reversibly: CuSO4.5H2O equilibrates with CuSO4 + 5H2O.
Mass loss on heating to constant mass, divided by water's Mr, gives the moles of water per formula unit.

low.restatement: The dot formula counts water molecules per formula unit; heating removes them and the mass drops.
low.analogy: Like a sponge whose soaked-in water is part of its shipped weight - dry it and the weight loss is the water's share.
low.examPointer: Quote the constant-mass requirement: heating stops only when two successive weighings agree.

medium.restatement: The mass lost on heating is the mass of xH2O; dividing that by 18.0 gives moles of water, and dividing the residue mass by the anhydrous Mr gives moles of salt - their ratio is x.
medium.analogy: It is the same divide-by-smallest logic as empirical formulae, with water as one 'element' and the salt as the other.
medium.examPointer: For 10.0 g hydrated copper(II) sulfate leaving 5.59 g residue: water = 4.41 g = 0.245 mol; salt = 5.59/159.6 = 0.035 mol; ratio 7, so CuSO4.7H2O.

check.stem: What does the formula CuSO4.5H2O state?

options.text: Each formula unit of copper(II) sulfate carries five waters of crystallisation
options.explanation: The dot formula counts five water molecules per copper sulfate unit.

options.text: The compound is a mixture of CuSO4 and H2O in a beaker
options.explanation: The water is bonded into the crystal lattice, not mixed in.
The subscript applies to water, not copper.

options.text: The salt contains exactly five water molecules as impurity
options.explanation: The water is structural, not contamination.

check.stem: Which term describes CuSO4 after all its water of crystallisation has been removed?

options.explanation: The anhydrous salt is the water-free residue CuSO4.
Hydrated describes the salt WITH its water.
Dissolving is unrelated to lattice water.
Aqueous means dissolved in water, a different state entirely.

check.stem: In the hydration equilibrium CuSO4.5H2O <=> CuSO4 + 5H2O, what drives the forward shift when a hydrated salt is heated?

options.text: Heat supplies the energy that expels water vapour from the crystal
options.explanation: Heating pushes water out of the lattice, shifting toward the anhydrous side.

options.text: Cooling condenses the water inside the crystal
options.explanation: Cooling favours hydration, the reverse shift.

options.text: The salt decomposes into copper and sulfur
options.explanation: No decomposition occurs; only water is lost.

options.text: Oxygen is absorbed from the air
options.explanation: Air plays no part in this equilibrium.

check.stem: Why must a hydrated salt be heated to CONSTANT mass before the calculation?

options.text: To ensure all the water of crystallisation has been driven off
options.explanation: Two agreeing successive weighings certify complete dehydration.

options.text: To make the salt melt evenly
options.explanation: Melting is not involved.
Constant mass certifies water loss, not purity.
The requirement concerns the sample, not the balance.

check.stem: 10.0 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate leaves 5.59 g of anhydrous solid. What is the mass of water lost?

options.explanation: 10.0 - 5.59 = 4.41 g of water driven off.
That is the residue, not the loss.
Masses subtract, not add.
The subtraction is wrong; 10.0 - 5.59 = 4.41.

check.stem: Define water of crystallisation.
check.modelAnswer: Water molecules that form part of a crystal's structure, written into the formula after a dot, as in CuSO4.5H2O.

check.stem: State the masses and moles needed to find x in CuSO4.xH2O from a heating experiment.
check.modelAnswer: You need the mass lost (divided by 18.0 to give moles of water) and the residue mass (divided by 159.6 to give moles of CuSO4); the mole ratio is x.

check.stem: Explain why the degree of hydration can differ for the same salt, citing cobalt(II) chloride.
check.modelAnswer: Crystal lattices can host different numbers of water molecules depending on how the structure packs, so cobalt(II) chloride exists as CoCl2.6H2O and CoCl2.2H2O - both are legitimate hydrated forms with different dot counts.

check.stem: 10.0 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated to constant mass, leaving 5.59 g. Determine the formula of the hydrate (Mr: CuSO4 159.6, H2O 18.0).
check.modelAnswer: Water lost = 4.41 g = 0.245 mol; salt = 5.59 / 159.6 = 0.035 mol; ratio 0.245 / 0.035 = 7, so the hydrate is CuSO4.7H2O.

glossary.definition: The simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound.
The exact count of each element's atoms in one molecule, equal to the empirical formula scaled by n.
Water molecules built into a crystal lattice and written after a dot in the formula.

workedExample.prompt: 10.0 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, heated to constant mass, leaves 5.59 g of anhydrous solid. Determine the formula of the hydrate. (Mr: CuSO4 = 159.6, H2O = 18.0)
steps: Divide by the smaller: water 0.245 / 0.035 = 7, salt 1.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The hydrate is CuSO4.7H2O - seven waters of crystallisation per formula unit.
